title: The Moon has a New Once-in-a-Century Crater - Nautilus
gist: NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter imaged a once-in-a-century lunar impact from spring 2024: a crater 728 feet wide and 141 feet deep, surrounded by a four-mile zone about 16 degrees Fahrenheit cooler. Science Advances papers use it to show the moon's surface churns ('impact gardening') far faster than once thought.

insights.claim: In spring 2024 the moon was hit by an object about as big as a six-story building, which left a new crater 728 feet wide and 141 feet deep.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Impactor sizes and frequency matter for the risk to lunar surface infrastructure and landers.

insights.claim: Authors in Science Advances describe a lunar impact this large as statistically rare, happening about once a century and effectively a once-in-a-lifetime observation.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Gives a benchmark for large-impact risk in lunar base planning.

insights.claim: The Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, in orbit for 17 years, surveys the moon with a wide-angle camera and flags images by software; most flags are false positives, but NASA specialist Robert Wagner spotted this crater in 2025.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Shows the value of long-lived orbital assets and automated change detection combined with human review.
insights.quote: It was by far the most obvious impact debris pattern I’ve ever seen in one of these images.

insights.claim: NASA moved from LRO's wide-angle camera to its narrow-angle camera for measurement, and then to the Diviner thermal instrument for temperature mapping.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: A layered multi-sensor workflow for planetary change detection.

insights.claim: The four-mile area around the new crater is about 16 degrees Fahrenheit cooler than the surrounding lunar surface, a pattern common for craters larger than 20 meters because impacts decompact regolith, and the looser material retains heat less well.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Regolith thermal properties matter for lunar construction, landing sites, and resource extraction.

insights.claim: 'Impact gardening' overturns the top half inch or so of lunar soil about once every 80,000 years, much faster than the old estimate of once every 10 million years.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: The lunar surface is more dynamic than assumed, which affects assumptions about surface stability for lunar infrastructure and dust exposure.
